# Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations

**Document No.:** ACAD-CG-2025-02
**Effective Date:** May 1, 2025
**Issuing Office:** Office of the Superintendent, Acadia National Park, Bar Harbor, ME
**Supersedes:** ACAD-CG-2021-04

(continues in Section 1, Scope) These regulations govern camping and fire use within Acadia National Park, including Blackwoods, Seawall, and Schoodic Woods campgrounds, the Duck Harbor campground on Isle au Haut, and all other Park lands on Mount Desert Island, the Schoodic Peninsula, and outlying islands.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 1. Scope

These regulations govern camping and fire use within Acadia National Park, including Blackwoods, Seawall, and Schoodic Woods campgrounds, the Duck Harbor campground on Isle au Haut, and all other Park lands on Mount Desert Island, the Schoodic Peninsula, and outlying islands. They implement 36 CFR 2.10 and 2.13 and the Superintendent's Compendium.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Designated campground site" means a numbered campsite within Blackwoods, Seawall, Schoodic Woods, or Duck Harbor campgrounds.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Designated campground site"** means a numbered campsite within Blackwoods, Seawall, Schoodic Woods, or Duck Harbor campgrounds.
- **"Established fireplace"** means the NPS-installed fire ring, grate, or stone fireplace at a designated campground site or designated picnic area.
- **"Backcountry"** means all Park lands outside designated campgrounds, picnic areas, and roads.
- **"Portable stove"** means a manufactured appliance burning pressurized gas or liquid fuel.

(continues in Section 3, Camping — General) Overnight camping within Acadia National Park is permitted only at designated campground sites.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 3. Camping — General

3.1 Overnight camping within Acadia National Park is permitted only at designated campground sites. There is no backcountry, dispersed, or at-large camping anywhere in the Park, in any season. This restriction reflects the Park's small land area, private inholdings, and fragile thin-soil ecosystems.

3.2 All campground sites require reservations through Recreation.gov. Blackwoods and Seawall operate May through mid-October; Schoodic Woods late May through Columbus Day; Duck Harbor by special reservation mid-May through mid-October, with access by mailboat from Stonington.

3.3 Maximum occupancy is six persons per standard site. Maximum stay is 14 nights per calendar year across all Park campgrounds combined.

3.4 Sleeping in vehicles at trailheads, parking areas, carriage road entrances, or along the Park Loop Road is prohibited and enforced year-round.

3.5 Quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. Generator use is limited to 8:00 a.m. through 8:00 p.m. at Schoodic Woods and prohibited entirely at Duck Harbor.

(continues in 4.1) Wood and charcoal fires are permitted only in established fireplaces at designated campground sites and at the designated picnic areas listed in Appendix A (Thompson Island, Pretty Marsh, Frazer Point, and Seawall picnic areas).

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 4. Fires

4.1 Wood and charcoal fires are permitted only in established fireplaces at designated campground sites and at the designated picnic areas listed in Appendix A (Thompson Island, Pretty Marsh, Frazer Point, and Seawall picnic areas). Fires at any other location in the Park, including beaches, summits, gravel bars, and all backcountry areas, are prohibited at all times.

(continues in 4.2-3) Because camping itself is confined to campgrounds under Section 3.1, there is no circumstance in which an overnight fire is lawful outside an established campground fireplace.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 4. Fires

4.2 Because camping itself is confined to campgrounds under Section 3.1, there is no circumstance in which an overnight fire is lawful outside an established campground fireplace.

4.3 Fires must be attended at all times and fully extinguished with water before the site is vacated or occupants sleep. During posted high fire danger, the Superintendent may suspend all open fires parkwide, including in campgrounds; suspension notices are posted at campground entrances and ranger stations.

(continues in 4.4-5) Portable stoves are permitted at campground sites and picnic areas.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 4. Fires

4.4 Portable stoves are permitted at campground sites and picnic areas. Stove use elsewhere in the Park (e.g., for day-hike cooking on summits) is permitted only at the designated picnic areas, not on trails or summits.

4.5 Firewood may not be brought into the Park from outside the State of Maine, and out-of-state visitors may not transport firewood into Maine under state quarantine law. Certified heat-treated firewood and firewood purchased locally are permitted. Gathering of dead and down wood within the Park is prohibited; all firewood must be purchased.

(continues in Section 5, Food Storage and Wildlife) All food, coolers, and scented items must be stored in a closed vehicle or provided storage when not in use.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 5. Food Storage and Wildlife

5.1 All food, coolers, and scented items must be stored in a closed vehicle or provided storage when not in use. While Acadia does not host grizzly bears, black bears, raccoons, and gulls routinely raid unsecured food.

5.2 Feeding any wildlife, including gulls at Thunder Hole and Sand Beach, is prohibited under 36 CFR 2.2.

(continues in Section 6, Campground-Specific Provisions) Blackwoods: no hookups; one vehicle per site plus one small tent trailer; showers available outside the Park in Otter Creek.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 6. Campground-Specific Provisions

6.1 Blackwoods: no hookups; one vehicle per site plus one small tent trailer; showers available outside the Park in Otter Creek.

6.2 Seawall: walk-in tent sites (section D) require carrying equipment up to 200 feet from parking.

6.3 Schoodic Woods: the only campground with electric and water hookups; RV limit 45 feet.

6.4 Duck Harbor: five lean-to shelters only; tents must be pitched inside lean-tos; open fires prohibited at Duck Harbor notwithstanding Section 4.1 — portable stoves only, due to the absence of fire suppression resources on Isle au Haut.

(continues in Section 7, Winter Camping) Blackwoods Campground remains open for primitive winter camping December 1 through March 31 by free permit obtained at Park Headquarters, walk-in only from the Route 3 gate.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 7. Winter Camping

7.1 Blackwoods Campground remains open for primitive winter camping December 1 through March 31 by free permit obtained at Park Headquarters, walk-in only from the Route 3 gate. Fires are permitted only in the established fireplaces of the designated winter sites; snow does not suspend Section 4.1.

(continues in Section 8, Relationship to Other Documents) Trail and carriage road conduct is governed by ACAD-CR-2025-05, Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 8. Relationship to Other Documents

Trail and carriage road conduct is governed by ACAD-CR-2025-05, *Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide*. Seasonal closures, including the Cadillac Summit Road vehicle reservation system, are published in ACAD-CL-2026-01, *Seasonal Closures and Access Notice*. Plain-language guidance appears in ACAD-FAQ-2026-01.

(continues in Section 9, Enforcement) Camping or fires outside the locations authorized by these regulations are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6 by fines up to $5,000 and/or six months' imprisonment.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 9. Enforcement

Camping or fires outside the locations authorized by these regulations are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6 by fines up to $5,000 and/or six months' imprisonment. Illegal fire scars on granite summits are treated as resource damage with restitution assessed for restoration costs.

(continues in Section 10, Contact) Campground information: (207) 288-3338. Reservations: Recreation.gov.

[Acadia National Park — Campfire and Campground Regulations]

## 10. Contact

Campground information: (207) 288-3338. Reservations: Recreation.gov. Fire danger status is posted daily at campground kiosks and the Hulls Cove Visitor Center.

# Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide

**Document No.:** ACAD-CR-2025-05
**Effective Date:** June 1, 2025
**Issuing Office:** Division of Resource and Visitor Protection, Acadia National Park

(continues in Section 1, Purpose) This guide establishes use rules for the 45-mile carriage road system and the maintained hiking trail network of Acadia National Park.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 1. Purpose

This guide establishes use rules for the 45-mile carriage road system and the maintained hiking trail network of Acadia National Park. It implements 36 CFR 1.5, 2.16, and 4.30, and the Superintendent's Compendium. Camping and fire rules are outside its scope; see ACAD-CG-2025-02, *Campfire and Campground Regulations*. Seasonal surface closures are announced under ACAD-CL-2026-01.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Carriage road" means the crushed-stone motor-free road system constructed 1913–1940, within Park boundaries.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Carriage road"** means the crushed-stone motor-free road system constructed 1913–1940, within Park boundaries.
- **"Connector"** means a carriage road segment on private land of the Land & Garden Preserve (Little Long Pond area), open to the public subject to the owner's posted rules.
- **"Class 1 e-bike"** means an electric bicycle with pedal-assist only, ceasing assistance at 20 mph.
- **"Mud season closure"** means a temporary closure of carriage roads during spring thaw to prevent surface damage.

(continues in Section 3, Permitted and Prohibited Uses — Carriage Roads) Permitted on all Park carriage roads: pedestrians, non-motorized bicycles, Class 1 e-bikes, equestrians (except as posted around Eagle Lake), and, in winter, skiers and snowshoers.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 3. Permitted and Prohibited Uses — Carriage Roads

3.1 Permitted on all Park carriage roads: pedestrians, non-motorized bicycles, Class 1 e-bikes, equestrians (except as posted around Eagle Lake), and, in winter, skiers and snowshoers.

3.2 Prohibited on all carriage roads: motor vehicles (except administrative and emergency), Class 2 and Class 3 e-bikes, motorized scooters and skateboards, and horse-drawn vehicles other than those operated under concession contract from Wildwood Stables.

3.3 On connectors within the Land & Garden Preserve, bicycles (including all e-bikes) are prohibited where posted; Preserve rules control on Preserve land.

3.4 Cyclists must yield to pedestrians and equestrians, announce when passing, and observe the posted 20 mph limit, reduced to 10 mph on descents with limited sight lines as signed.

3.5 Pets are permitted on carriage roads on a leash not exceeding six feet.

(continues in Section 4, Hiking Trails) Bicycles are prohibited on all hiking trails.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 4. Hiking Trails

4.1 Bicycles are prohibited on all hiking trails.

4.2 Pets are permitted on most hiking trails on a six-foot maximum leash, but are prohibited on ladder trails (Precipice, Beehive, Ladder Trail on Dorr Mountain, Jordan Cliffs, Beech Cliffs) and on Sand Beach and Echo Lake Beach in season.

4.3 Trail structures, including iron rungs and ladders, must be used as installed; bypassing them on vegetation is prohibited.

4.4 The Precipice, Jordan Cliffs, and Valley Cove trails are typically closed March through mid-August for peregrine falcon nesting; exact dates are set annually in ACAD-CL-2026-01, Section 4.

4.5 Summit vegetation on Cadillac, Sargent, and other open summits is protected; travel is restricted to bare rock and marked routes above treeline signage.

(continues in Section 5, Winter Use) When snow cover is present, designated carriage road segments are groomed for classic skiing by volunteer partners.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 5. Winter Use

5.1 When snow cover is present, designated carriage road segments are groomed for classic skiing by volunteer partners. Walkers and snowshoers must not travel in set ski tracks on groomed segments.

5.2 Bicycles, including fat-tire bicycles, are prohibited on groomed segments while grooming is in effect, and on all carriage roads during a posted mud season closure.

5.3 The Park Loop Road closes to vehicles December 1 through April 14 (except the Ocean Drive and Jordan Pond access segments) and is available for skiing, walking, and cycling during the closure; ice conditions are not monitored.

(continues in Section 6, Mud Season and Surface Protection) Each spring, typically mid-March through late April, carriage roads are closed to all bicycles and equestrians (and to pedestrians where posted) during thaw.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 6. Mud Season and Surface Protection

6.1 Each spring, typically mid-March through late April, carriage roads are closed to all bicycles and equestrians (and to pedestrians where posted) during thaw. Use of soft carriage road surfaces causes rutting requiring costly repair; closure status is updated weekly during the season and posted at all major entrances and in ACAD-CL-2026-01.

6.2 Year-round, travel off the carriage road surface to bypass puddles or gates is prohibited where posted for shoulder revegetation.

(continues in Section 7, Equestrian Use) Equestrian use is permitted on carriage roads except the Eagle Lake loop and Witch Hole Pond loop as posted.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 7. Equestrian Use

7.1 Equestrian use is permitted on carriage roads except the Eagle Lake loop and Witch Hole Pond loop as posted. Riders must remove manure from the traveled surface at gates and intersections.

7.2 Overnight stabling is available only through Wildwood Stables; horses may not be kept overnight at campgrounds.

(continues in Section 8, Accessibility) The carriage road system's grades generally do not exceed 8 percent; the Eagle Lake and Jordan Pond loops are the most commonly recommended for wheelchair and adaptive-cycle users.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 8. Accessibility

8.1 The carriage road system's grades generally do not exceed 8 percent; the Eagle Lake and Jordan Pond loops are the most commonly recommended for wheelchair and adaptive-cycle users. Motorized wheelchairs and OPDMDs used by persons with mobility disabilities are permitted under 36 CFR 1.5 determinations posted at the Hulls Cove Visitor Center.

(continues in Section 9, Events and Groups) Organized events (races, rides, or groups exceeding 25 persons) on carriage roads require a special use permit from the Office of the Superintendent, applied for at least four weeks in advance.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 9. Events and Groups

9.1 Organized events (races, rides, or groups exceeding 25 persons) on carriage roads require a special use permit from the Office of the Superintendent, applied for at least four weeks in advance.

9.2 Commercial bicycle touring operates under concession or CUA authorization only; clients must be accompanied by an authorized guide.

(continues in Section 10, Enforcement and Contact) Violations are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6. Rangers and mounted patrol enforce these rules; repeat e-bike class violations result in revocation of Park cycling privileges under the Compendium.

[Acadia National Park — Carriage Roads and Trails Use Guide]

## 10. Enforcement and Contact

Violations are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6. Rangers and mounted patrol enforce these rules; repeat e-bike class violations result in revocation of Park cycling privileges under the Compendium. Questions: (207) 288-3338, or the Hulls Cove Visitor Center. Plain-language answers appear in ACAD-FAQ-2026-01.

# Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026

**Document No.:** ACAD-CL-2026-01
**Effective Date:** January 1, 2026 (last revised June 1, 2026)
**Issuing Office:** Office of the Superintendent, Acadia National Park
**Status:** Living document; revised as conditions change.

(continues in Section 1, Purpose) This notice consolidates road, trail, and area closures and timed-access requirements in effect within Acadia National Park for 2026, issued under 36 CFR 1.5. Camping and fire restrictions appear in ACAD-CG-2025-02; carriage road and trail use rules in ACAD-CR-2025-05.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 1. Purpose

This notice consolidates road, trail, and area closures and timed-access requirements in effect within Acadia National Park for 2026, issued under 36 CFR 1.5. Camping and fire restrictions appear in ACAD-CG-2025-02; carriage road and trail use rules in ACAD-CR-2025-05.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Vehicle reservation" means a timed entry reservation purchased on Recreation.gov for the Cadillac Summit Road.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Vehicle reservation"** means a timed entry reservation purchased on Recreation.gov for the Cadillac Summit Road.
- **"Winter closure"** means the annual December 1 through April 14 closure of specified park roads to motor vehicles.
- **"Nesting closure"** means a wildlife closure under Section 4 protecting cliff-nesting raptors.

(continues in Section 3, Roads and Vehicle Reservations) Cadillac Summit Road: vehicle reservations are required for all private vehicles from May 20 through October 22, 2026, during all hours the road is open.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 3. Roads and Vehicle Reservations

3.1 **Cadillac Summit Road:** vehicle reservations are required for all private vehicles from May 20 through October 22, 2026, during all hours the road is open. Thirty percent of reservations are released 90 days ahead; seventy percent at 10:00 a.m. Eastern Time two days ahead. Walking and bicycling up the Summit Road require no reservation. The Summit Road is closed to all vehicles December 1 through April 14 and during posted high-wind and ice events in the shoulder seasons.

3.2 **Park Loop Road:** closed to motor vehicles December 1, 2025 through April 14, 2026, except the Ocean Drive segment (Sand Beach entrance to Otter Cliff Road) and the Jordan Pond access road, which remain open year-round, conditions permitting. Full loop reopened April 15, 2026.

3.3 **Schoodic Loop Road:** open year-round, weather permitting; one-way traffic pattern in effect at all times from Frazer Point.

3.4 **Seasonal gate schedule:** unpaved fire roads (Hio Road, Marshall Brook, Long Pond fire roads) are gated December 1 through spring grading, typically mid-May.

(continues in Section 4, Nesting Closures (Recurring)) Precipice Trail, Jordan Cliffs Trail, Valley Cove Trail, and the east face of Champlain Mountain: closed effective March 15, 2026, for peregrine falcon nesting.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 4. Nesting Closures (Recurring)

4.1 Precipice Trail, Jordan Cliffs Trail, Valley Cove Trail, and the east face of Champlain Mountain: closed effective March 15, 2026, for peregrine falcon nesting. The Precipice and Champlain east face closures were lifted August 5 in 2025; 2026 lifting will be announced by press release and posted at trailheads when chicks fledge.

4.2 Petit Manan and outer island seabird colonies (Schoodic district waters): landing prohibited April 1 through August 31 annually.

4.3 Sand Beach nesting area (piping plover, when present): symbolic fencing may close portions of the upper beach April through August; obey posted boundaries.

(continues in Section 5, Trail Closures — Temporary) Witch Hole Pond carriage road segment (posts 2–4): closed weekdays June 8 through July 3, 2026, for culvert replacement; open weekends.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 5. Trail Closures — Temporary

5.1 Witch Hole Pond carriage road segment (posts 2–4): closed weekdays June 8 through July 3, 2026, for culvert replacement; open weekends.

5.2 Ocean Path (Thunder Hole to Otter Point): single-lane pedestrian pattern in effect through June 2026 during rehabilitation of storm-damaged sections from the January 2024 coastal storms; expect flagger control on weekdays.

5.3 Bass Harbor Head Light Station grounds: open 9:00 a.m. to sunset; the parking area closes when full, typically by 4:00 p.m. in summer for sunset viewing. No roadside parking on Lighthouse Road.

(continues in Section 6, Mud Season) Carriage roads were closed to bicycles and equestrians March 12 through April 24, 2026, for spring thaw, under the authority described in ACAD-CR-2025-05, Section 6. All segments reopened April 25, 2026.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 6. Mud Season

6.1 Carriage roads were closed to bicycles and equestrians March 12 through April 24, 2026, for spring thaw, under the authority described in ACAD-CR-2025-05, Section 6. All segments reopened April 25, 2026.

(continues in Section 7, Water and Island Access) Echo Lake Beach and Sand Beach lifeguard season: June 20 through Labor Day 2026. Swimming outside lifeguard hours is at the visitor's own risk; water temperatures rarely exceed 60 °F at Sand Beach.

[Acadia National Park — Seasonal Closures and Access Notice, 2026]

## 7. Water and Island Access

7.1 Echo Lake Beach and Sand Beach lifeguard season: June 20 through Labor Day 2026. Swimming outside lifeguard hours is at the visitor's own risk; water temperatures rarely exceed 60 °F at Sand Beach.

7.2 Duck Harbor (Isle au Haut) mailboat service: May 15 through October 12, 2026. Day-use visitor numbers to the Isle au Haut district are capped under the Compendium; boat capacity effectively enforces the cap.

7.3 Lake Wood and Half Moon Pond road access: closed to vehicles in 2026 due to parking area rehabilitation; walk-in access remains open.

# Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions

**Document No.:** ACAD-FAQ-2026-01
**Effective Date:** April 1, 2026
**Issuing Office:** Division of Interpretation and Education, Acadia National Park

This document answers common questions for the 2026 season. It is informational only; the regulations cited control where any conflict exists.

(continues in Section 1, Entry and Cadillac Mountain) Q: Do I need a reservation to enter Acadia?

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 1. Entry and Cadillac Mountain

**Q: Do I need a reservation to enter Acadia?**
A: Not for the Park generally. A vehicle reservation is required only to drive the Cadillac Summit Road, from May 20 through October 22, 2026. A park entrance pass is required separately for all visitors. See ACAD-CL-2026-01, Section 3.1.

**Q: How do I get a Cadillac sunrise reservation?**
A: The same way as any Cadillac reservation: 30 percent are released 90 days ahead and 70 percent at 10:00 a.m. Eastern two days ahead, on Recreation.gov. Sunrise slots are the first to sell out, typically within minutes of the two-day release.

**Q: Can I hike or bike up Cadillac without a reservation?**
A: Yes. Reservations apply only to private vehicles on the Summit Road. The North Ridge and South Ridge trails and the road shoulder (for bicycles) require no reservation.

(continues in Section 2, Camping) Q: Can I backpack or camp in the backcountry?

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 2. Camping

**Q: Can I backpack or camp in the backcountry?**
A: No. Acadia has no backcountry or dispersed camping anywhere, in any season. Camping is permitted only at the four designated campgrounds (Blackwoods, Seawall, Schoodic Woods, and Duck Harbor on Isle au Haut), all by reservation. See ACAD-CG-2025-02, Section 3.

**Q: Can I sleep in my car at a trailhead?**
A: No. Overnight vehicle occupancy outside a registered campsite is prohibited and enforced year-round.

(continues in Section 3, Campfires) Q: Where can I have a campfire?

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 3. Campfires

**Q: Where can I have a campfire?**
A: Only in the installed fireplaces at designated campground sites and at four designated picnic areas (Thompson Island, Pretty Marsh, Frazer Point, Seawall). Fires anywhere else — beaches, summits, and all undeveloped areas — are prohibited at all times. Duck Harbor campground allows no fires at all; stoves only. See ACAD-CG-2025-02, Section 4.

**Q: Can I bring firewood from home?**
A: Not from out of state. Maine's firewood quarantine prohibits importing untreated firewood; buy certified heat-treated or local wood. Gathering wood inside the Park is also prohibited.

(continues in Section 4, Trails and Carriage Roads) Q: Can I ride an e-bike on the carriage roads?

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 4. Trails and Carriage Roads

**Q: Can I ride an e-bike on the carriage roads?**
A: Class 1 (pedal-assist) e-bikes only. Class 2 and 3 e-bikes are prohibited on carriage roads. All bicycles are prohibited on hiking trails and on the Land & Garden Preserve carriage roads where posted. See ACAD-CR-2025-05, Section 3.

**Q: Why is the Precipice Trail closed?**
A: Peregrine falcon nesting. The Precipice, Jordan Cliffs, and Valley Cove trails close each spring (March 15 in 2026) and reopen when chicks fledge, typically in early August. See ACAD-CL-2026-01, Section 4.

**Q: Are the ladder trails suitable for children or dogs?**
A: Ladder trails (Precipice, Beehive, and similar) involve exposed iron-rung climbing and are unsuitable for small children, and pets are prohibited on them. The Bowl via the Bowl Trail is the standard family alternative to the Beehive.

**Q: Can I bring my dog?**
A: Acadia is one of the more pet-friendly national parks: leashed pets (6-foot maximum) are allowed on most trails and carriage roads. Exceptions: ladder trails, Sand Beach and Echo Lake Beach in season, Duck Harbor Campground, and Wild Gardens of Acadia.

(continues in Section 5, Tides and Coastal Safety) Q: When can I walk the Bar Island land bridge?

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 5. Tides and Coastal Safety

**Q: When can I walk the Bar Island land bridge?**
A: Approximately 1.5 hours on either side of low tide. Visitors are stranded on Bar Island regularly; the wait for the next low tide is about nine hours, and emergency boat retrieval is billed to the visitor. Consult a tide chart, not a fixed clock time.

**Q: Is it safe to climb on rocks at Thunder Hole?**
A: Stay behind railings during any surf event. Rogue waves have swept visitors from the lower viewing area; the gates close during storm swell.

(continues in Section 6, Logistics) Q: Is there a free shuttle?

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 6. Logistics

**Q: Is there a free shuttle?**
A: The fare-free Island Explorer bus operates June 23 through Columbus Day 2026, connecting campgrounds, trailheads, and Bar Harbor. Bicycles are carried on select routes. The Island Explorer does not serve the Cadillac Summit Road.

**Q: Where do I get drinking water?**
A: Campgrounds, the Hulls Cove Visitor Center, and Jordan Pond House in season. Carry water for all hikes; summit trails have none. Swimming and wading are prohibited in Jordan Pond, the public water supply.

**Q: What are the quiet hours at campgrounds?**
A: 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. See ACAD-CG-2025-02, Section 3.5.

(continues in Section 7, Contact) General information: (207) 288-3338. Emergency: 911 (Bar Harbor dispatch covers the Park).

[Acadia National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 7. Contact

General information: (207) 288-3338. Emergency: 911 (Bar Harbor dispatch covers the Park). Current conditions are posted at the Hulls Cove Visitor Center and in ACAD-CL-2026-01.

# Glacier National Park — Backcountry Camping Guide

**Document No.:** GLAC-BC-2025-04
**Effective Date:** May 1, 2025 (revised January 15, 2026)
**Issuing Office:** Backcountry Office, Glacier National Park, West Glacier, MT
**Supersedes:** GLAC-BC-2023-02

(continues in Section 1, Purpose and Scope) This guide establishes the conditions under which overnight backcountry camping is authorized within Glacier National Park (the "Park").

[Glacier National Park — Backcountry Camping Guide]

## 1. Purpose and Scope

This guide establishes the conditions under which overnight backcountry camping is authorized within Glacier National Park (the "Park"). It applies to all persons camping outside of designated frontcountry campgrounds, including all designated backcountry campgrounds, the Sperry and Granite Park chalet areas, and undesignated-camping zones as defined in Section 2. Frontcountry camping is governed separately under GLAC-FC-2025-01, *Frontcountry Campground Regulations*. Permit issuance procedures are set out in GLAC-PERM-2026-01, *Backcountry Permit Regulations*, which should be read together with this guide.

This advisory sets out required and recommended practices for travel in grizzly and black bear habitat within Glacier National Park, and lists current elevated-activity notices. - **"Approved container"** means a bear-resistant food container listed by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee as of the effective date of this advisory.
- **"Attractant"** means any food, beverage, garbage, cookware, toiletry, or other scented item capable of drawing wildlife.

## 3. Required Practices — All Visitors

3.1 All attractants must be secured at all times when not in immediate use: in frontcountry areas, in a hard-sided vehicle or Park food locker (see GLAC-FC-2025-01, Section 5); in the backcountry, in an approved container or on a Park-installed hanging system (see GLAC-BC-2025-04, Section 3.5).

3.2 Feeding, baiting, or intentionally approaching within 100 yards of a bear is prohibited.

3.3 Visitors must report all bear encounters involving charging, contact, or loss of food to any ranger station within 24 hours.

(continues in Section 4, Recommended Practices — Trail Travel) Hike in groups of three or more.

## 4. Recommended Practices — Trail Travel

4.1 Hike in groups of three or more. Since 1980, no fatal bear attack in the Park has involved a group of four or more traveling together and making noise.

4.2 Carry bear spray in an immediately accessible holster, not inside a pack. Know its range (approximately 25 feet) and expiration date. Bear spray may not be carried on Park shuttles' exterior racks and may not be flown in carry-on or checked baggage.

4.3 Make noise, particularly near running water, in dense vegetation, and on blind corners. Bells alone are not considered adequate.

4.4 If you encounter a grizzly at close range and it has not charged, group together, speak calmly, and back away slowly. Do not run. If contact is imminent following a charge, use bear spray; if contact occurs, lie face down, protect the neck, and remain still.

3.3 Maximum stay is 14 nights parkwide between July 1 and Labor Day, and 30 nights in any calendar year.

Fires are permitted during this season unless the posted fire danger rating is Very High or Extreme, or unless a temporary fire restriction has been issued under the Superintendent's Compendium, in which case all wood fires are suspended parkwide until the restriction is lifted. Current fire danger ratings are posted at campground kiosks and entrance stations each morning.

# Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions

**Document No.:** GLAC-FAQ-2026-01
**Effective Date:** May 1, 2026
**Issuing Office:** Division of Interpretation and Education, Glacier National Park

This document answers common visitor questions for the 2026 season. It is informational only; where it conflicts with a regulation or the Superintendent's Compendium, the regulation controls. Cross-referenced documents are available at visitor centers and on the Park website.

(continues in Section 1, Entry and Reservations) Q: Do I need a vehicle reservation to enter the Park in 2026? A: Yes, for some corridors.

[Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 1. Entry and Reservations

**Q: Do I need a vehicle reservation to enter the Park in 2026?**
A: Yes, for some corridors. Between June 13 and September 28, 2026, a timed vehicle reservation is required to enter the Going-to-the-Sun Road corridor from the west side and the Many Glacier corridor between 6:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. Reservations are released on Recreation.gov 120 days in advance, with a next-day block released at 7:00 p.m. Mountain Time. Entry before 6:00 a.m. or after 3:00 p.m. does not require a reservation. A park entrance pass is required in all cases and is separate from the reservation.

**Q: Is the Going-to-the-Sun Road open?**
A: The alpine section opened June 27, 2026. Typical full-road season is late June or early July through the third week of October, weather depending. See GLAC-CL-2026-01, *Seasonal Closures and Trail Status*, Section 3, for current road status.

(continues in Section 2, Trails and Conditions) Q: Can I hike to Avalanche Lake?

[Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 2. Trails and Conditions

**Q: Can I hike to Avalanche Lake?**
A: Not at present. The Avalanche Lake Trail is closed effective June 20, 2026, until further notice, because the footbridge over Avalanche Creek washed out in mid-June 2026. The Trail of the Cedars loop remains open. See GLAC-CL-2026-01, Section 4.1. No reopening date has been announced.

**Q: Is Hidden Meadow Trail open?**
A: It is open with restrictions. Because of grizzly bear activity reported in late June 2026, hikers must travel in groups of four or more and off-trail travel near the meadow is prohibited. See GLAC-WL-2026-02, *Bear Safety Advisory*, Section 5.1.

**Q: When is the snow gone from high trails?**
A: Passes typically melt out between mid-July and early August. Gunsight Pass and Swiftcurrent Pass hold snow the longest. Check trail status boards at visitor centers.

(continues in Section 3, Camping and Permits) Q: How do I get a backcountry permit for 2026? A: Advance reservations were allocated by lottery, with applications accepted March 1–15, 2026, on Recreation.gov.

[Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 3. Camping and Permits

**Q: How do I get a backcountry permit for 2026?**
A: Advance reservations were allocated by lottery, with applications accepted March 1–15, 2026, on Recreation.gov. If you missed the lottery, unclaimed inventory went on sale April 15, and walk-up permits are issued in person starting 24 hours before your trip at the Apgar Backcountry Permit Center and other listed stations. Maximum party size is eight. See GLAC-PERM-2026-01, *Backcountry Permit Regulations*.

**Q: Do I need a permit to camp in a regular campground?**
A: No permit, but you need a site registration, and Fish Creek, Many Glacier, and St. Mary require reservations in peak season. See GLAC-FC-2025-01, *Frontcountry Campground Regulations*.

(continues in Section 4, Campfires) Q: Can I have a campfire at my campground?

[Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 4. Campfires

**Q: Can I have a campfire at my campground?**
A: In frontcountry campgrounds, yes, in the designated fire ring at your site, between May 15 and September 30, unless the fire danger rating is Very High or Extreme or a temporary restriction is in effect. In the backcountry, it depends entirely on the specific campsite: some backcountry campgrounds allow fires in installed rings, while others prohibit wood fires year-round regardless of conditions. Check the designation for your exact campsite on the backcountry map when your permit is issued, and see GLAC-BC-2025-04, *Backcountry Camping Guide*, Section 4.

**Q: Can I bring my own firewood?**
A: Only firewood purchased within Flathead, Glacier, or Pondera counties may be brought into the Park, under the Montana firewood quarantine.

(continues in Section 5, Wildlife) Q: Do I need bear spray?

[Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 5. Wildlife

**Q: Do I need bear spray?**
A: It is not legally required, but the Park strongly recommends that every hiking party carry it and know how to use it. Rental and purchase locations are available in Apgar and St. Mary. See GLAC-WL-2026-02 for required food-storage practices, which are mandatory.

**Q: What do I do if I see a bear on the trail?**
A: Do not run. Group together, speak calmly, back away, and give the bear an escape route. Report any close encounter or charge to a ranger station within 24 hours.

(continues in Section 6, Pets, Drones, and Miscellaneous) Q: Can I bring my dog on trails?

[Glacier National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 6. Pets, Drones, and Miscellaneous

**Q: Can I bring my dog on trails?**
A: No. Pets are permitted only in developed areas, along roads, and in campgrounds, on a leash no longer than six feet. They are not permitted on any trail.

**Q: Are drones allowed?**
A: No. Launching, landing, or operating unmanned aircraft within the Park is prohibited.

**Q: Is there cell service?**
A: Coverage is minimal outside Apgar, West Glacier, and St. Mary. Do not rely on a phone for backcountry emergencies; the Park recommends carrying a satellite communicator.

**Q: Where can I fill water bottles?**
A: Potable water is available seasonally at visitor centers and most frontcountry campgrounds. All surface water in the backcountry must be filtered, boiled, or chemically treated.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 1. General Requirement

1.1 A backcountry permit and advance reservation are required for all overnight stays in the backcountry of Great Smoky Mountains National Park, year-round. Camping is permitted only at designated backcountry campsites (numbered 1 through 113) and shelters; dispersed camping is prohibited parkwide.

1.2 Reservations and permits are obtained through the Park's online backcountry permit system up to 30 days in advance. The fee is $8 per person per night, capped at $40 per person per trip. There is no lottery; inventory is continuous first-come.

1.3 The permit must be in the trip leader's possession (printed or on a device with adequate battery) and produced on request.

1.4 Fire rules for backcountry sites appear in GRSM-FIRE-2025-02, *Fire Regulations*, Section 4, and differ from the frontcountry rules in that document.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Campsite" means a designated, numbered backcountry campsite shown on the official trail map.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Campsite"** means a designated, numbered backcountry campsite shown on the official trail map.
- **"Shelter"** means one of the 15 stone or frame shelters, 12 of which lie on the Appalachian Trail corridor.
- **"AT thru-hiker"** means a person holding a valid Appalachian Trail thru-hiker permit under Section 6.
- **"Food storage cable"** means the pulley-and-cable system installed at every campsite and shelter for suspending food.

(continues in Section 3, Reservations and Occupancy) Maximum party size is 8 persons at most campsites and shelters.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 3. Reservations and Occupancy

3.1 Maximum party size is 8 persons at most campsites and shelters. A limited list of large-group sites accepts up to 12; group limits are enforced by the reservation system.

3.2 Maximum stay is 3 consecutive nights at any campsite, and 1 night at any shelter.

3.3 Tenting adjacent to a shelter is prohibited except by AT thru-hikers when the shelter is full.

3.4 Reservations are site- and date-specific. Itinerary changes must be made through the permit system or by telephone to the Backcountry Information Office before the affected night.

3.5 Occupancy of a campsite without a reservation for that site and night is a citable offense even where space is available.

(continues in Section 4, Food Storage) All food, trash, and scented items must be suspended on the provided food storage cables at all times when not in immediate use, or stored in a hard-sided container approved by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee (accepted parkwide although the Park's bears are black bears).

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 4. Food Storage

4.1 All food, trash, and scented items must be suspended on the provided food storage cables at all times when not in immediate use, or stored in a hard-sided container approved by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee (accepted parkwide although the Park's bears are black bears).

4.2 Food storage violations are the leading cause of campsite closures. Sites closed for bear activity are posted on the permit system and the backcountry conditions page; reservations at closed sites are cancelled with refund.

(continues in Section 5, Water and Sanitation) All water sources must be treated.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 5. Water and Sanitation

5.1 All water sources must be treated. Springs marked on the trail map are seasonal; several ridge-crest sites (including campsites 13, 26, and the Icewater Spring shelter in late summer) require water carries of up to one mile.

5.2 Human waste must be buried six inches deep at least 100 feet from water, campsites, and trails. Toilet paper must be buried or packed out. Privies at shelters must be used where present.

5.3 Washing with soap in any stream is prohibited.

(continues in Section 6, Appalachian Trail Thru-Hikers) Hikers beginning and ending their trip at least 50 miles outside the Park, traveling only on the AT corridor, may obtain the AT thru-hiker permit ($40, valid 38 days) in lieu of site-specific reservations.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 6. Appalachian Trail Thru-Hikers

6.1 Hikers beginning and ending their trip at least 50 miles outside the Park, traveling only on the AT corridor, may obtain the AT thru-hiker permit ($40, valid 38 days) in lieu of site-specific reservations.

6.2 Thru-hikers must stay at shelters, moving in one direction, no more than one night per shelter; when a shelter is full, tenting within sight of the shelter is authorized.

(continues in Section 7, Horse and Stock Use) Stock are permitted only on designated horse trails and at designated horse campsites, which include hitch racks.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 7. Horse and Stock Use

7.1 Stock are permitted only on designated horse trails and at designated horse campsites, which include hitch racks. Stock may not be tied to trees or held within 100 feet of water.

7.2 Parties with stock are limited to 8 persons and 8 head of stock. Certified weed-free feed is required; grazing is prohibited.

(continues in Section 8, Seasonal Considerations) High-elevation sites (above 4,500 feet, including all AT shelters east of Newfound Gap) receive snow and ice from November through early April; traction devices and zero-degree equipment are advised in winter.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 8. Seasonal Considerations

8.1 High-elevation sites (above 4,500 feet, including all AT shelters east of Newfound Gap) receive snow and ice from November through early April; traction devices and zero-degree equipment are advised in winter.

8.2 Stream crossings without bridges, particularly on Hazel Creek, Forney Creek, and Eagle Creek trails, become impassable after heavy rain. The Park does not rate crossings; turn back when water exceeds knee depth.

8.3 Road access to trailheads varies seasonally; Clingmans Dome Road closes December 1 through March 31, and secondary roads (Parson Branch, Heintooga Ridge) close seasonally as posted in GRSM-FAQ-2026-01 and on the Park's road status page.

(continues in Section 9, Enforcement) Camping outside designated sites, occupying an unreserved site, or violating food storage requirements is punishable under 36 CFR 1.6 and 2.10. Backcountry rangers patrol the AT corridor and high-use drainages regularly.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide]

## 1. Purpose

These regulations govern all open fires, charcoal fires, and stove use within Great Smoky Mountains National Park, implementing 36 CFR 2.13 and the Superintendent's Compendium. Following the November 2016 Chimney Tops 2 fire, fire management within the Park is subject to heightened enforcement; visitors should treat every provision of this document as strictly enforced.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Established fire ring" means an NPS-installed steel ring or grate at a frontcountry campground or picnic pavilion, or the constructed fire ring maintained at a designated backcountry campsite or shelter.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Fire Regulations]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Established fire ring"** means an NPS-installed steel ring or grate at a frontcountry campground or picnic pavilion, or the constructed fire ring maintained at a designated backcountry campsite or shelter.
- **"Heat-treated firewood"** means firewood bundled and certified by the USDA or a state agency as heat-treated to kill pests.
- **"Fire danger rating"** means the rating (Low through Extreme) posted daily at visitor centers and campground kiosks.
- **"Burn ban"** means a temporary prohibition on some or all fire types issued under Section 6.

(continues in Section 3, Frontcountry Fires) Fires in frontcountry campgrounds (including Cades Cove, Elkmont, Smokemont, Deep Creek, Cosby, and Balsam Mountain) and picnic areas are permitted only in established fire rings and grates, at any hour, unless a burn ban is in effect.

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Fire Regulations]

## 3. Frontcountry Fires

3.1 Fires in frontcountry campgrounds (including Cades Cove, Elkmont, Smokemont, Deep Creek, Cosby, and Balsam Mountain) and picnic areas are permitted only in established fire rings and grates, at any hour, unless a burn ban is in effect.

3.2 Only heat-treated certified firewood may be brought into the Park. Untreated firewood may not cross the Park boundary regardless of origin, including from adjacent counties. Dead and down wood may be collected within the Park for immediate use in frontcountry campgrounds.

3.3 Fires must be attended at all times and extinguished with water until cold before occupants sleep or vacate the site.

(continues in Section 4, Backcountry Fires) Fires at designated backcountry campsites and shelters are permitted only in the established fire ring at each site, using only dead and down wood collected in the vicinity, unless a burn ban is in effect.

## 4. Backcountry Fires

# Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions

**Document No.:** GRSM-FAQ-2026-01
**Effective Date:** March 1, 2026
**Issuing Office:** Division of Interpretation, Great Smoky Mountains National Park

This document answers common visitor questions for 2026. It is informational; the cited regulations control where any conflict exists.

(continues in Section 1, Entry, Parking, and Roads) Q: Is there an entrance fee?

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 1. Entry, Parking, and Roads

**Q: Is there an entrance fee?**
A: No entrance fee is charged, a condition of the Park's founding deeds. However, a parking tag is required for any vehicle parked longer than 15 minutes anywhere in the Park: $5 daily, $15 weekly, or $40 annual, available online and at visitor centers. The tag is per vehicle, not per person, and does not guarantee a space.

**Q: Do I need a reservation to enter?**
A: No. The Park has no timed-entry system in 2026. Popular areas (Laurel Falls, Cades Cove, Clingmans Dome) fill early on peak days; arrive before 9:00 a.m. or after 3:00 p.m.

**Q: When is Cades Cove Loop Road vehicle-free?**
A: Every Wednesday from May 6 through September 30, 2026, the loop is closed to motor vehicles and open to bicycles and pedestrians all day.

**Q: Which roads close in winter?**
A: Clingmans Dome Road closes December 1 through March 31 annually. Parson Branch, Rich Mountain, Heintooga Ridge, and Balsam Mountain roads close seasonally as posted. Newfound Gap Road (US 441) remains open but closes temporarily for snow and ice at any time November through March; check the road status line at (865) 436-1200, option 2.

(continues in Section 2, Camping) Q: How do I camp in the backcountry?

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 2. Camping

**Q: How do I camp in the backcountry?**
A: Reserve a specific numbered campsite or shelter up to 30 days ahead at smokiespermits.nps.gov ($8 per person per night, $40 trip cap). Camping is allowed only at designated sites; there is no dispersed camping. Party limit is 8 at most sites. See GRSM-BC-2025-01, *Backcountry Camping and Permit Guide*.

**Q: Can I just show up and camp?**
A: Not in the backcountry; every night requires a site-specific reservation, even in winter. Frontcountry campgrounds accept reservations on Recreation.gov, and some sites are same-day if unsold.

**Q: Are there bears?**
A: Approximately 1,900 black bears, one of the densest populations in the eastern United States. Food and scented items must be hung on the cables provided at every backcountry site or stored as directed in frontcountry campgrounds. Food storage violations carry fines and are the leading cause of campsite closures.

(continues in Section 3, Campfires) Q: Can I have a campfire while backpacking?

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 3. Campfires

**Q: Can I have a campfire while backpacking?**
A: Yes, at the established fire ring at your designated campsite or shelter, using dead and down wood gathered nearby, unless a burn ban is posted. Fires anywhere other than an established ring are always prohibited. Note that autumn is this Park's peak fire season, and Stage 1 bans (no backcountry fires) are common in October and November. See GRSM-FIRE-2025-02, Section 4.

**Q: Can I bring firewood into the Park?**
A: Only certified heat-treated firewood may cross the Park boundary. Untreated firewood is prohibited regardless of where it was cut. You may gather dead and down wood inside the Park for immediate use.

(continues in Section 4, Trails) Q: How do I hike to Clingmans Dome (Kuwohi)?

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 4. Trails

**Q: How do I hike to Clingmans Dome (Kuwohi)?**
A: The paved half-mile trail from the parking area climbs steeply to the observation tower. The parking area requires the standard parking tag. When Clingmans Dome Road is closed (December through March), the tower is reachable only by a 7-mile ski or hike from Newfound Gap.

**Q: Is Laurel Falls Trail open?**
A: The Laurel Falls corridor is operating under a pilot congestion plan in 2026; expect posted parking limits on weekends. Check current status at the Sugarlands Visitor Center.

**Q: Are dogs allowed on trails?**
A: No, with two exceptions: the Gatlinburg Trail and the Oconaluftee River Trail, on leash. Dogs are otherwise limited to campgrounds and road corridors.

(continues in Section 5, Wildlife) Q: What do I do if I see a bear?

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 5. Wildlife

**Q: What do I do if I see a bear?**
A: Keep at least 50 yards away; willfully approaching closer is illegal. If a bear approaches you, stand your ground, make noise, and appear large; do not run and do not drop food. Report aggressive bears to (865) 436-1230.

**Q: When can I see synchronous fireflies?**
A: The Elkmont firefly viewing event runs approximately eight nights in late May or early June (dates announced each April). Access is by lottery-issued vehicle pass only; the 2026 lottery ran April 24 through 27.

**Q: Are elk dangerous?**
A: Elk in the Cataloochee and Oconaluftee areas are wild and unpredictable, particularly during the autumn rut. Remain 50 yards away; parking on road shoulders to view elk is restricted as posted.

(continues in Section 6, Miscellaneous) Q: Is there cell service?

[Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 6. Miscellaneous

**Q: Is there cell service?**
A: Coverage is largely absent inside the Park. Download maps in advance. Emergency calls sometimes connect on ridge crests; Park dispatch is (865) 436-9171.

**Q: Can I fish?**
A: Yes, year-round, with a valid Tennessee or North Carolina license (either is valid parkwide). Brook trout possession rules and single-hook artificial-lure requirements apply; see the fishing regulations sheet at any visitor center.

**Q: Where are the visitor centers?**
A: Sugarlands (near Gatlinburg), Oconaluftee (near Cherokee), Cades Cove, and Clingmans Dome (seasonal).

## 1. Purpose

These regulations govern open fires, charcoal, and stove use within Rocky Mountain National Park, implementing 36 CFR 2.13 and the Superintendent's Compendium. The Park's fire posture reflects the 2020 East Troublesome fire, which burned approximately 30,000 acres within Park boundaries; several provisions below are more restrictive than those of neighboring jurisdictions, and visitors should not assume that rules from adjacent National Forest lands apply inside the Park.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Developed area fire site" means an NPS-installed fire ring or grate at a frontcountry campground site or at a picnic area listed in Appendix A. - "Wilderness campsite" means a designated backcountry campsite administered under ROMO-WC-2026-01, Wilderness Camping Guide.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Fire Restrictions and Stove Regulations]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Developed area fire site"** means an NPS-installed fire ring or grate at a frontcountry campground site or at a picnic area listed in Appendix A.
- **"Wilderness campsite"** means a designated backcountry campsite administered under ROMO-WC-2026-01, *Wilderness Camping Guide*.
- **"Open fire"** means any wood, charcoal, or unpressurized-solid-fuel fire, including twig stoves.
- **"Pressurized stove"** means a manufactured appliance burning pressurized gas or liquid fuel with an on/off valve.

(continues in Section 3, Baseline Rules — Frontcountry) Open fires are permitted only in developed area fire sites at the following campgrounds: Moraine Park, Glacier Basin, Aspenglen, Timber Creek, and Longs Peak, and at the picnic areas listed in Appendix A (including Sprague Lake, Endovalley, and Hidden Valley).

## 3. Baseline Rules — Frontcountry

3.1 Open fires are permitted only in developed area fire sites at the following campgrounds: Moraine Park, Glacier Basin, Aspenglen, Timber Creek, and Longs Peak, and at the picnic areas listed in Appendix A (including Sprague Lake, Endovalley, and Hidden Valley).

3.2 Fires must remain within the installed ring or grate, be attended continuously, and be extinguished with water until cold to the touch.

3.3 Only purchased firewood or dead and down wood collected outside the Park may be burned; gathering wood within the Park is prohibited in all areas, frontcountry and wilderness alike. Firewood transported from areas under emerald ash borer quarantine must be certified heat-treated.

(continues in Section 4, Baseline Rules — Wilderness) Open fires are prohibited at all wilderness campsites and throughout the Park's designated wilderness, with the sole exception of the specific sites listed in Appendix B as "fire sites," each of which is equipped with a metal fire ring.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Fire Restrictions and Stove Regulations]

## 4. Baseline Rules — Wilderness

4.1 Open fires are prohibited at all wilderness campsites and throughout the Park's designated wilderness, with the sole exception of the specific sites listed in Appendix B as "fire sites," each of which is equipped with a metal fire ring. As of the effective date, fewer than a dozen of the Park's roughly 120 wilderness campsites are Appendix B fire sites, all below 9,500 feet on the east side.

4.2 At all other wilderness campsites, and everywhere above 9,500 feet, open fires are prohibited year-round regardless of fire danger. Pressurized stoves are permitted at all wilderness campsites except during a Stage 3 restriction under Section 5.

4.3 Fires at Appendix B fire sites are suspended automatically whenever the posted fire danger is Very High or Extreme, and during any staged restriction.

(continues in Section 5, Staged Restrictions) The Superintendent may declare staged restrictions based on fuel conditions, weather, and regional fire activity: - Stage 1: All open fires prohibited parkwide, including Appendix B fire sites; developed area fire sites permitted for charcoal and wood.

## 5. Staged Restrictions

5.1 The Superintendent may declare staged restrictions based on fuel conditions, weather, and regional fire activity:

- **Stage 1:** All open fires prohibited parkwide, including Appendix B fire sites; developed area fire sites permitted for charcoal and wood.
- **Stage 2:** All open fires prohibited parkwide, including developed area fire sites; pressurized stoves permitted.
- **Stage 3:** All ignition sources prohibited except pressurized stoves within developed campgrounds; smoking prohibited except in enclosed vehicles.

5.2 Declarations are posted at entrance stations, wilderness offices, campground kiosks, and the Park website, and are typically coordinated with, but not identical to, restrictions on the surrounding Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests. Where Park and Forest stages differ, the Park's declaration controls within Park boundaries.

5.3 Stage 1 or higher restrictions have been in effect for some portion of every summer since 2018; visitors planning July through September trips should expect wilderness fire prohibitions to be effectively total.

(continues in Section 6, Prohibited Acts — All Areas, All Times) Parkwide, at all times: fires outside installed rings and grates; unattended fires; burning garbage or food waste; fireworks; sky lanterns; exploding targets; and the use of any accelerant other than commercial fire starters.

## 6. Prohibited Acts — All Areas, All Times

6.1 Parkwide, at all times: fires outside installed rings and grates; unattended fires; burning garbage or food waste; fireworks; sky lanterns; exploding targets; and the use of any accelerant other than commercial fire starters.

6.2 Smoking is prohibited on all trails and within the wilderness at all times, except at wilderness campsites in an area cleared to mineral soil, and is further restricted during staged restrictions per Section 5.1.

6.3 Operating a charcoal grill anywhere other than a developed area fire site is prohibited, including in parking areas and on the Trail Ridge Road corridor.

(continues in Section 7, Elevation and Alpine Considerations) Approximately one-third of the Park lies above treeline.

## 7. Elevation and Alpine Considerations

7.1 Approximately one-third of the Park lies above treeline. In alpine tundra, all open flame, including pressurized stoves, must be operated on bare rock or gravel; operating any flame on tundra vegetation is prohibited and treated as resource damage.

7.2 High winds along the Continental Divide can carry embers substantial distances; the Superintendent may impose localized fire suspensions in wind events without a full staged declaration.

Violations are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6 and 2.13 by fines up to $5,000 and six months' imprisonment. Persons whose fires escape are liable for suppression costs; following East Troublesome, the Park refers all escaped-fire cases for prosecution.

## 1. Timed Entry Basics

**Q: Do I need a timed entry reservation in 2026?**
A: Yes, for most daytime entries between May 22 and October 19, 2026. Two reservation types exist:

1. **Park Access+ (Bear Lake Road Corridor):** required 5:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Covers the Bear Lake Road corridor and the rest of the Park.
2. **Park Access (rest of Park):** required 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Covers everything except the Bear Lake Road corridor, including Trail Ridge Road, the Wild Basin and Longs Peak areas, and the west side.

Entering outside the stated windows requires no reservation. An entrance pass is required in all cases and is separate.

**Q: When are reservations released?**
A: On Recreation.gov at 8:00 a.m. Mountain Time on the first day of the preceding month (June reservations released May 1, and so on), with approximately 40 percent of inventory held back and released at 7:00 p.m. the night before each entry date.

**Q: How long is my reservation valid?**
A: It admits one vehicle within a two-hour entry window. Once inside, you may remain for the rest of the day and re-enter that same day with your receipt.

(continues in Section 2, Exceptions and Edge Cases) Q: I have a wilderness camping permit.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Timed Entry and Visitor FAQ, 2026]

## 2. Exceptions and Edge Cases

**Q: I have a wilderness camping permit. Do I need a timed entry reservation?**
A: No, for the day your permit begins. A wilderness permit issued under ROMO-WC-2026-01 serves as your entry authorization for the trip's start date, at any entrance, at any hour. Display the permit on your dashboard at the authorized trailhead.

**Q: I have a campground reservation inside the Park.**
A: Your campground confirmation admits you on check-in day without a separate timed entry reservation.

**Q: What about entering before 5:00 a.m. to climb Longs Peak?**
A: Entries before 5:00 a.m. require no reservation, and most Keyhole Route parties start between 2:00 and 4:00 a.m. for lightning-safety reasons in any case. Note that the non-technical season on the Keyhole Route is short; see ROMO-WC-2026-01, Section 7.3.

**Q: Can I ride a bicycle or walk in without a reservation?**
A: Yes. Timed entry applies to motor vehicles only. Cyclists on Trail Ridge Road should carry layers; the road crosses 12,183 feet and weather changes rapidly.

(continues in Section 3, Roads and Seasons) Q: When does Trail Ridge Road open?

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Timed Entry and Visitor FAQ, 2026]

## 3. Roads and Seasons

**Q: When does Trail Ridge Road open?**
A: Typically by Memorial Day weekend, weather permitting, closing for the season in mid-October after the first sustained storms. In 2026, the road opened fully on May 23. Temporary day closures for snow occur in every month; call the recorded status line at (970) 586-1222.

**Q: Is Old Fall River Road open?**
A: The one-way uphill historic route typically opens July 1 through late September, 2026 dates conditions permitting. Vehicles over 25 feet and all trailers are prohibited.

(continues in Section 4, Camping and Fires) Q: How do I camp overnight in the backcountry?

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Timed Entry and Visitor FAQ, 2026]

## 4. Camping and Fires

**Q: How do I camp overnight in the backcountry?**
A: Reserve a designated wilderness campsite (season inventory opened March 2, 2026, on Recreation.gov; $36 per trip). Party limit is 7 at standard sites. A bear-resistant container is required May through October. See ROMO-WC-2026-01, *Wilderness Camping Guide*.

**Q: Can I have a campfire in the backcountry?**
A: Almost certainly not. Open fires are prohibited at all but a small list of designated east-side wilderness fire sites below 9,500 feet, and even those are suspended when fire danger is Very High or during the staged restrictions that have applied in some part of every recent summer. Above 9,500 feet the prohibition is year-round and unconditional. Pressurized-gas stoves are permitted at all sites outside a Stage 3 restriction. See ROMO-FIRE-2025-01, Section 4.

**Q: Where can I have a fire in the frontcountry?**
A: In the installed rings at the five drive-in campgrounds and listed picnic areas, unless a staged restriction is posted. Wood gathering inside the Park is prohibited everywhere; bring certified or locally purchased wood.

(continues in Section 5, Safety and Wildlife) Q: What is the biggest hazard in the Park?

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Timed Entry and Visitor FAQ, 2026]

## 5. Safety and Wildlife

**Q: What is the biggest hazard in the Park?**
A: Afternoon lightning above treeline, July through early September. Plan to be below treeline by noon on Trail Ridge Road area trails and summit routes.

**Q: How close can I get to elk and moose?**
A: Stay 25 yards from elk and moose (75 yards during the autumn elk rut, when meadow closures are posted in Moraine Park and Horseshoe Park). Moose in the Kawuneeche Valley injure visitors more often than any other species on the west side.

**Q: Is there cell coverage?**
A: Intermittent on the east side, largely absent on the west side and in wilderness. Do not rely on a phone for emergencies.

## 1. General Requirement

1.1 A wilderness camping permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry of Rocky Mountain National Park, year-round. Camping is permitted only at designated wilderness campsites, in designated cross-country zones, or at winter bivouac locations authorized under Section 7.

1.2 Permits specify sites and nights and must be carried by the trip leader. The permit itself does not exempt the holder's vehicle from the timed entry reservation system where in effect; see ROMO-FAQ-2026-01 for entry rules and the trailhead-parking exception.

1.3 Fire use at wilderness campsites is governed by ROMO-FIRE-2025-01, Section 4; the substantial majority of sites prohibit open fires entirely.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Designated site" means a numbered wilderness campsite marked with a silver arrowhead post.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Wilderness Camping Guide]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Designated site"** means a numbered wilderness campsite marked with a silver arrowhead post.
- **"Cross-country zone"** means one of the mapped zones where parties camp at undeveloped locations subject to Section 5.
- **"Stock site"** means a designated site equipped for horses and llamas.
- **"Technical bivouac"** means an overnight stay on a climbing route under Section 7.2.

(continues in Section 3, Permits and Reservations) Reservations for the May 1 through October 31, 2026 season open on Recreation.gov at 8:00 a.m. Mountain Time on March 2, 2026, for the entire season.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Wilderness Camping Guide]

## 3. Permits and Reservations

3.1 Reservations for the May 1 through October 31, 2026 season open on Recreation.gov at 8:00 a.m. Mountain Time on March 2, 2026, for the entire season. There is no lottery; inventory is continuous.

3.2 The administrative fee is $36 per trip, non-refundable. Winter permits (November 1 through April 30) are free and issued in person or by telephone.

3.3 Unreserved capacity is issued in person at the Beaver Meadows and Kawuneeche wilderness offices beginning the day before the trip start.

3.4 Maximum party size is 7 persons at standard designated sites and 12 at designated group sites. Cross-country zone parties may not exceed 7.

3.5 Maximum stay: 3 consecutive nights at any one site, 7 total wilderness nights June 1 through September 30, and 14 nights in the remainder of the year.

(continues in Section 4, Conduct at Designated Sites) Tents must be pitched within the impacted core of the site, identified by the arrowhead post, and never on vegetation.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Wilderness Camping Guide]

## 4. Conduct at Designated Sites

4.1 Tents must be pitched within the impacted core of the site, identified by the arrowhead post, and never on vegetation.

4.2 All food, trash, and scented items must be stored in a hard-sided bear-resistant container from May 1 through October 31 parkwide. Hanging is not an accepted method in this Park; trees at and above subalpine elevations do not reliably provide compliant geometry.

4.3 Water sources: maintain all camp activities, including stove operation and dishwashing, at least 100 feet from lakes and streams.

4.4 Privies exist at a minority of high-use sites (including Thunder Lake, Ouzel Lake, and Lawn Lake); elsewhere, bury human waste six inches deep 200 feet from water. Above treeline, all solid human waste must be packed out using a carry-out kit; burial is not permitted in alpine terrain.

(continues in Section 5, Cross-Country Zones) Cross-country zone camping is intended for experienced parties.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Wilderness Camping Guide]

## 5. Cross-Country Zones

5.1 Cross-country zone camping is intended for experienced parties. Camps must be at least 200 feet from water and trails, out of sight of other parties where terrain permits, below treeline unless the permit states otherwise, and moved at least one mile each night within the zone.

5.2 Open fires are prohibited in all cross-country zones without exception (see ROMO-FIRE-2025-01, Section 4.2).

(continues in Section 6, Stock Use) Stock parties are limited to designated stock sites and to trails posted open to stock.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Wilderness Camping Guide]

## 6. Stock Use

6.1 Stock parties are limited to designated stock sites and to trails posted open to stock. Llamas are regulated as stock. Party limit is 8 head.

6.2 Certified weed-free feed is required within the Park; grazing is prohibited everywhere.

(continues in Section 7, Winter and Technical Use) Winter camping (November 1 through April 30) is permitted in winter zones above designated snow depth, subject to the free winter permit.

[Rocky Mountain National Park — Wilderness Camping Guide]

## 7. Winter and Technical Use

7.1 Winter camping (November 1 through April 30) is permitted in winter zones above designated snow depth, subject to the free winter permit. Avalanche terrain is not marked; parties are responsible for their own hazard evaluation.

7.2 Technical bivouacs on routes of Grade IV or longer (including the Diamond on Longs Peak) are authorized under a bivouac endorsement to the wilderness permit, limited to the face or ledge system named on the permit.

## 1. Purpose

These regulations govern the use of campfires, charcoal fires, and portable stoves throughout Yosemite National Park. They implement 36 CFR 2.13 and the Superintendent's Compendium. Wilderness camping conduct generally is addressed in YOSE-WILD-2026-01, *Wilderness Permit and Trip Planning Guide*; this document is the controlling authority on fire.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Campfire" means any open wood or charcoal fire.

[Yosemite National Park — Campfire and Stove Regulations]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Campfire"** means any open wood or charcoal fire.
- **"Established fire ring"** means a pre-existing rock fire ring in wilderness, or an NPS-installed fire ring or grate in a developed campground.
- **"Portable stove"** means a manufactured appliance burning pressurized gas, liquid fuel, or solid fuel tablets, capable of being switched off.
- **"Valley floor"** means the developed area of Yosemite Valley below the 4,600-foot contour.

(continues in Section 3, Developed Campgrounds and Picnic Areas) Campfires in developed campgrounds are permitted only in NPS-installed fire rings and grates.

[Yosemite National Park — Campfire and Stove Regulations]

## 3. Developed Campgrounds and Picnic Areas

3.1 Campfires in developed campgrounds are permitted only in NPS-installed fire rings and grates.

3.2 On the Valley floor, campfires (including charcoal) are permitted only between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. from May 1 through September 30, in order to limit evening smoke accumulation under inversion conditions. Outside those hours during that period, no new fuel may be added and fires must be extinguished. From October 1 through April 30, Valley floor campfires are permitted at any hour, conditions permitting.

3.3 Outside Yosemite Valley, campground campfires are permitted at any hour unless a restriction under Section 6 is in effect.

3.4 Only dead and down wood may be gathered, and only outside Yosemite Valley and outside sequoia groves; wood gathering is prohibited on the Valley floor and above 9,600 feet. Imported firewood must comply with California's invasive-pest advisories.

(continues in Section 4, Wilderness Fires) In wilderness areas of the Park, campfires are permitted only in established fire rings, and only at elevations below 9,600 feet.

[Yosemite National Park — Campfire and Stove Regulations]

## 4. Wilderness Fires

4.1 In wilderness areas of the Park, campfires are permitted only in established fire rings, and only at elevations below 9,600 feet. Campfires are prohibited above 9,600 feet throughout the Park, year-round, due to slow-growing subalpine fuels. This elevation prohibition does not vary with fire danger and is not subject to waiver.

4.2 Certain drainages below 9,600 feet are additionally closed to fires as posted, including within 0.25 miles of Laurel Lake outflow and in the Merced Lake shoreline zone; consult the wilderness trailhead postings and YOSE-WILD-2026-01, Appendix B.

4.3 Construction of new fire rings is prohibited. Where an established ring exists, it must be used as found; enlarging a ring is prohibited.

4.4 Wilderness fires must be attended at all times, kept smaller than three feet in diameter, and extinguished with water until cold to the touch. Burying a fire does not satisfy this requirement.

(continues in Section 5, Stoves) Portable stoves are permitted throughout the Park, including above 9,600 feet, except during a Stage 3 restriction under Section 6. 5.2 A California Campfire Permit is required to operate a stove or fire in wilderness; the permit is issued automatically with a Yosemite wilderness permit

[Yosemite National Park — Campfire and Stove Regulations]

## 5. Stoves

5.1 Portable stoves are permitted throughout the Park, including above 9,600 feet, except during a Stage 3 restriction under Section 6.

5.2 A California Campfire Permit is required to operate a stove or fire in wilderness; the permit is issued automatically with a Yosemite wilderness permit and is otherwise available free online.

5.3 Twig-burning stoves and other appliances that burn unpressurized solid biomass are regulated as campfires, not as stoves, and are therefore prohibited above 9,600 feet and wherever campfires are restricted.

(continues in Section 6, Temporary Fire Restrictions) The Superintendent may impose staged restrictions based on fuel moisture, weather, and fire activity: - Stage 1: Wilderness campfires prohibited parkwide; campground fires permitted.

[Yosemite National Park — Campfire and Stove Regulations]

## 6. Temporary Fire Restrictions

6.1 The Superintendent may impose staged restrictions based on fuel moisture, weather, and fire activity:

- **Stage 1:** Wilderness campfires prohibited parkwide; campground fires permitted.
- **Stage 2:** All campfires prohibited parkwide, including developed campgrounds; portable gas stoves permitted.
- **Stage 3:** All ignition sources prohibited except pressurized-gas stoves in developed campgrounds only.

6.2 Restrictions are posted at entrance stations, wilderness centers, and on the Park website, and take precedence over Sections 3 and 4 wherever more restrictive.

6.3 Smoking is prohibited whenever Stage 1 or higher is in effect, except within an enclosed vehicle or building, or in a developed area cleared of flammable material.

(continues in Section 7, Prohibited Acts) The following are prohibited at all times, parkwide: fires outside established rings; fires left unattended; burning of garbage, food waste, or non-wood materials; fires within sequoia groves; and the use of accelerants other than commercial fire starters.

## 7. Prohibited Acts

7.1 The following are prohibited at all times, parkwide: fires outside established rings; fires left unattended; burning of garbage, food waste, or non-wood materials; fires within sequoia groves; and the use of accelerants other than commercial fire starters.

7.2 Violation of this document is punishable under 36 CFR 1.6 and 2.13 by a fine of up to $5,000, imprisonment up to six months, or both, and by liability for suppression costs where a violation results in a wildfire.
