# Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions

**Document No.:** YOSE-FAQ-2026-01
**Effective Date:** March 1, 2026
**Issuing Office:** Division of Interpretation, Yosemite National Park

This document is a plain-language summary for the 2026 season. It does not replace the regulations it summarizes; where it conflicts with YOSE-FIRE-2025-02, YOSE-WILD-2026-01, or the Superintendent's Compendium, those documents control.

(continues in Section 1, Getting In) Q: Do I need a reservation to drive into Yosemite in 2026? A: Yes, on peak dates.

[Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 1. Getting In

**Q: Do I need a reservation to drive into Yosemite in 2026?**
A: Yes, on peak dates. A vehicle reservation is required to enter between 6:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. on weekends and holidays from May 23 through June 14, daily from June 15 through August 16, and weekends through October 12, 2026. Visitors with lodging, campground, or wilderness permit confirmations are exempt for the dates of their stay. Reservations are separate from the entrance fee.

**Q: Is Tioga Road open?**
A: Tioga Road (Highway 120 through the park) typically opens between late May and early July and closes with the first major snowfall, usually November. Glacier Point Road usually opens in May. Check the Park's road conditions line at (209) 372-0200 for current status; closures are documented in YOSE-CL-2026-01.

(continues in Section 2, Camping) Q: How do I get a campsite in Yosemite Valley?

[Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 2. Camping

**Q: How do I get a campsite in Yosemite Valley?**
A: All Valley campgrounds are reservation-only. Reservations open on Recreation.gov five months in advance in one-month blocks at 7:00 a.m. Pacific Time and typically sell out within minutes. Cancellations are re-released continuously, so checking repeatedly is worthwhile.

**Q: Can I sleep in my car?**
A: Only within a numbered campsite you are registered to. Sleeping in vehicles at pullouts, trailhead lots, or along roads is prohibited.

(continues in Section 3, Campfires) Q: Can I have a campfire at my campsite?

[Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 3. Campfires

**Q: Can I have a campfire at my campsite?**
A: In developed campgrounds, yes, in the installed fire ring, but note the Valley floor hours: from May 1 through September 30, fires on the Valley floor are allowed only between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. Campgrounds outside the Valley have no hour restriction unless a temporary fire restriction is in effect. See YOSE-FIRE-2025-02, Section 3.

**Q: Can I have a campfire while backpacking?**
A: Only below 9,600 feet elevation, and only in an already-established fire ring. Above 9,600 feet, campfires are prohibited year-round everywhere in the Park. Gas stoves are fine at any elevation outside the most severe restriction stage. During dry periods the Superintendent may ban wilderness fires entirely, so check the current restriction stage when you pick up your permit. See YOSE-FIRE-2025-02, Sections 4 through 6.

**Q: Do I need any kind of fire permit?**
A: A California Campfire Permit is required for any stove or fire in wilderness. It is included automatically with your Yosemite wilderness permit.

(continues in Section 4, Wilderness Trips) Q: How far in advance do I need a wilderness permit?

[Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 4. Wilderness Trips

**Q: How far in advance do I need a wilderness permit?**
A: Reservations open by lottery 24 weeks before your entry date and popular trailheads (Happy Isles, Cathedral Lakes, Lyell Canyon) fill immediately. Forty percent of each trailhead's quota is held back for in-person issuance starting at 11:00 a.m. the day before entry. See YOSE-WILD-2026-01, Section 2.

**Q: Do I really need a bear canister?**
A: Yes. An approved bear-resistant container is required for all overnight wilderness stays, everywhere in the Park, in every season. Hanging food is not an accepted alternative in Yosemite. Rentals are available at wilderness centers.

**Q: How do I climb Half Dome?**
A: The cables are typically up from the Friday before Memorial Day through the second Monday of October. Day hikers need a Half Dome permit from the preseason lottery (March) or the two-day-in-advance daily lottery. Backpackers request a Half Dome rider with their wilderness permit.

(continues in Section 5, Wildlife and Safety) Q: Are there grizzly bears in Yosemite?

[Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 5. Wildlife and Safety

**Q: Are there grizzly bears in Yosemite?**
A: No. Yosemite has only American black bears. They are, however, highly skilled at obtaining human food. Never leave food in your vehicle overnight in the Valley; use the food lockers at trailheads and campsites. Improper food storage is a citable offense.

**Q: Is the water safe to drink?**
A: Tap water in developed areas is potable. All lake, river, and stream water should be treated before drinking.

**Q: Are drones allowed?**
A: No. Operating unmanned aircraft is prohibited throughout the Park.

(continues in Section 6, Miscellaneous) Q: Where can I see giant sequoias?

[Yosemite National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 6. Miscellaneous

**Q: Where can I see giant sequoias?**
A: Mariposa Grove (largest, served by shuttle from the Welcome Plaza), Tuolumne Grove, and Merced Grove. Overnight camping is prohibited in all groves, and fires are prohibited within grove boundaries at all times.

**Q: Can I swim in the Merced River?**
A: Yes, in most reaches when conditions are safe, except within 100 feet of designated riparian restoration zones as posted. Swimming is prohibited above Vernal and Nevada Falls and in Hetch Hetchy Reservoir.

**Q: What if I have questions this document does not answer?**
A: Call (209) 372-0200 or ask at any visitor center. Wilderness-specific questions: (209) 372-0740.

## 1. General Requirement

1.1 A wilderness permit is required year-round for all overnight stays in the Yosemite Wilderness. Day hiking does not require a permit, with the exception of the Half Dome cables, which require a Half Dome permit for day use.

1.2 Permits are issued per trailhead and entry date under a quota system. The permit must be carried by the trip leader and produced on request.

(continues in Section 2, Reservations) Sixty percent of each trailhead quota is reservable by weekly lottery on Recreation.gov, opening 24 weeks (168 days) before the entry date and running for one week.

[Yosemite National Park — Wilderness Permit and Trip Planning Guide]

## 2. Reservations

2.1 Sixty percent of each trailhead quota is reservable by weekly lottery on Recreation.gov, opening 24 weeks (168 days) before the entry date and running for one week. Remaining reservable inventory after each lottery is available first-come on-line until seven days before entry.

2.2 The reservation fee is $10 per confirmation plus $5 per person. Fees are non-refundable.

2.3 Forty percent of each quota is held for in-person issuance beginning at 11:00 a.m. the day before entry at the wilderness centers in Yosemite Valley, Tuolumne Meadows, Wawona, Big Oak Flat, and Hetch Hetchy.

2.4 Half Dome ascent by wilderness permit holders requires the Half Dome rider requested with the reservation ($10 per person if awarded).

(continues in Section 3, Itinerary Rules) The permit fixes the entry trailhead and date and the first night's camping zone.

[Yosemite National Park — Wilderness Permit and Trip Planning Guide]

## 3. Itinerary Rules

3.1 The permit fixes the entry trailhead and date and the first night's camping zone. Subsequent nights are flexible within the Wilderness, subject to the closures in YOSE-CL-2026-01, *Seasonal Closures and Access Notice*.

3.2 The first night must be spent at least four trail miles from any trailhead, and outside the no-camping zones posted for the Little Yosemite Valley corridor except within the designated Little Yosemite Valley campground.

3.3 Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of any water body or trail, above the posted treeline camping limits, and within one mile of any road or developed area.

3.4 Maximum group size is 15 persons on trail, and 8 persons for any party traveling off-trail or camping in a cross-country zone.

3.5 Maximum stay is 14 consecutive nights in the Wilderness, and no more than 2 consecutive nights in the Little Yosemite Valley campground.

(continues in Section 4, Trailhead Access and Parking) Overnight parking is authorized only in signed backpacker lots at each trailhead; the permit number must be displayed on the dashboard.

## 4. Trailhead Access and Parking

4.1 Overnight parking is authorized only in signed backpacker lots at each trailhead; the permit number must be displayed on the dashboard.

4.2 Permit holders may spend the night before and the night after their trip in the backpacker campgrounds (Valley, Tuolumne Meadows, Wawona, Hetch Hetchy) for the posted nightly fee, one night on each end, without a separate campground reservation.

4.3 Holders entering via Tuolumne Meadows should note that Tioga Road typically opens between late May and early July; permits for entries before the road opening are issued conditionally.

(continues in Section 5, Food Storage) An allowed bear-resistant food container is required for all overnight stays in the Yosemite Wilderness, parkwide, year-round.

[Yosemite National Park — Wilderness Permit and Trip Planning Guide]

## 5. Food Storage

5.1 An allowed bear-resistant food container is required for all overnight stays in the Yosemite Wilderness, parkwide, year-round. Counterbalance hanging does not satisfy this requirement anywhere in the Park.

5.2 All food, trash, and scented items must be stored in the container whenever they are more than an arm's reach away, including while sleeping and during side trips.

5.3 Containers must be from the Park's allowed list as of the trip date; rental containers are available at wilderness centers for a nominal fee with deposit.

5.4 In the Little Yosemite Valley and Merced Lake corridors, NPS food lockers, where present, may be used in lieu of containers while camped at those sites.

6.2 All toilet paper and hygiene products must be packed out. Burning toilet paper is prohibited (see YOSE-FIRE-2025-02, Section 7).

6.3 Washing with soap, including biodegradable soap, directly in any water body is prohibited.

**Effective Date:** March 1, 2025
**Issuing Office:** Wilderness and Backcountry Office, Zion National Park, Springdale, UT
**Supersedes:** ZION-BC-2022-01

(continues in Section 1, Scope) These regulations govern overnight and technical day use of the backcountry and designated wilderness of Zion National Park, including designated backcountry campsites, at-large camping zones, and technical canyoneering routes.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 1. Scope

These regulations govern overnight and technical day use of the backcountry and designated wilderness of Zion National Park, including designated backcountry campsites, at-large camping zones, and technical canyoneering routes. Permit reservation procedures for the Virgin River Narrows are detailed separately in ZION-NAR-2026-01, *Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide*. Frontcountry campgrounds (Watchman, South, Lava Point) are governed by posted campground rules and are outside the scope of this document.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Backcountry" means all Park lands more than 100 feet from a paved road or developed area, excluding frontcountry campgrounds.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Backcountry"** means all Park lands more than 100 feet from a paved road or developed area, excluding frontcountry campgrounds.
- **"Designated site"** means a numbered campsite along the West Rim, La Verkin Creek, Hop Valley, or Narrows corridors.
- **"At-large zone"** means an area where camping is permitted at any compliant location, as mapped in the current Wilderness Guide.
- **"Technical route"** means any route requiring rappelling or other rope work, including all slot canyons subject to permit.
- **"Stove"** means a manufactured appliance burning pressurized gas or liquid fuel that can be switched off.

(continues in Section 3, Permits) A wilderness permit is required for: all overnight backcountry stays; all technical routes; and all through-hikes of the Virgin River Narrows from Chamberlain's Ranch.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 3. Permits

3.1 A wilderness permit is required for: all overnight backcountry stays; all technical routes; and all through-hikes of the Virgin River Narrows from Chamberlain's Ranch.

3.2 Advance reservations are available on the Park's permit system up to two months ahead (released on the 5th of each month at 10:00 a.m. Mountain Time); last-minute drawing requests are accepted 2 to 7 days before the trip date; remaining spaces are issued in person the day before or day of the trip at the Zion Canyon Wilderness Desk.

3.3 Maximum group size is 12 persons for most areas, and 6 persons in designated slot canyons and the Subway (Left Fork) corridor. Groups may not split and recombine to evade these limits.

3.4 Permits must be carried and produced on request. Itineraries are fixed as to site and night for designated sites.

(continues in Section 4, Fires) Wood and charcoal fires, including twig stoves and any device burning unpressurized biomass, are prohibited throughout the backcountry of Zion National Park at all times, in all seasons, at all elevations, and under all fire-danger conditions.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 4. Fires

4.1 Wood and charcoal fires, including twig stoves and any device burning unpressurized biomass, are prohibited throughout the backcountry of Zion National Park at all times, in all seasons, at all elevations, and under all fire-danger conditions. There is no season, site, or condition under which a backcountry campfire is authorized in this Park.

4.2 Pressurized-gas and liquid-fuel stoves are permitted in the backcountry, except during a total fire ban declared under the Superintendent's Compendium, during which the Compendium's terms control.

4.3 Wood fires in frontcountry campgrounds are permitted only in installed fire rings and grills at Watchman and South campgrounds, subject to posted seasonal restrictions; this allowance does not extend to Lava Point, where fires are prohibited when posted during dry periods.

4.4 Possession of firewood in the backcountry is prohibited.

(continues in Section 5, Camping Conduct) In at-large zones, camps must be located out of sight of any trail, at least 200 feet from any water source or archaeological site, and at least one mile from any road or trailhead unless the zone map states otherwise.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 5. Camping Conduct

5.1 In at-large zones, camps must be located out of sight of any trail, at least 200 feet from any water source or archaeological site, and at least one mile from any road or trailhead unless the zone map states otherwise.

5.2 Camping is prohibited: within Zion Canyon between the Temple of Sinawava and the South Campground; on the West Rim Trail outside designated sites; within 100 feet of any spring; and anywhere within the Left Fork (Subway) corridor.

5.3 Maximum stay is three consecutive nights at any designated site or within any single at-large zone, and 14 backcountry nights per calendar year per person.

5.4 Quiet hours (10:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.) apply at all designated sites.

(continues in Section 6, Water, Sanitation, and Waste) All human waste in the Narrows corridor, the Left Fork corridor, and all slot canyons must be packed out using a commercial waste containment system; disposal kits are available at the Wilderness Desk.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 6. Water, Sanitation, and Waste

6.1 All human waste in the Narrows corridor, the Left Fork corridor, and all slot canyons must be packed out using a commercial waste containment system; disposal kits are available at the Wilderness Desk. Elsewhere, waste must be buried six inches deep at least 200 feet from water.

6.2 All trash and toilet paper must be packed out parkwide. Burying or burning refuse is prohibited (see Section 4.1).

6.3 Springs are the sole reliable water sources on plateau routes; consult the Wilderness Desk for current flow status. All water must be treated. During cyanobacteria advisories on the Virgin River, filtering does not render the water safe; carry all water for Narrows trips when an advisory is posted.

(continues in Section 7, Hazards Specific to This Park) Flash floods are the principal hazard in all canyon routes.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 7. Hazards Specific to This Park

7.1 Flash floods are the principal hazard in all canyon routes. Permits for the Narrows and technical canyons are suspended automatically when the National Weather Service issues a flash flood warning for the area, and may be suspended under a flash flood watch at the discretion of the Wilderness Desk. See ZION-NAR-2026-01, Section 6.

7.2 Summer plateau and canyon temperatures regularly exceed 100 °F; each hiker on exposed routes should carry a minimum of one gallon of water per day.

7.3 Cliff edges on the West Rim and Angels Landing routes are unfenced. Angels Landing beyond Scout Lookout requires a separate day-use permit issued by seasonal lottery.

(continues in Section 8, Enforcement) Violations of these regulations, including the fire prohibition in Section 4.1, are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6, 2.10, and 2.13. Rangers patrol backcountry corridors regularly, and fire scars are investigated as resource damage with restitution assessed.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 8. Enforcement

Violations of these regulations, including the fire prohibition in Section 4.1, are punishable under 36 CFR 1.6, 2.10, and 2.13. Rangers patrol backcountry corridors regularly, and fire scars are investigated as resource damage with restitution assessed.

(continues in Section 9, Contact) Zion Canyon Wilderness Desk: (435) 772-0170. Current advisories, water source status, and same-day permit availability are posted at the desk each morning.

[Zion National Park — Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations]

## 9. Contact

Zion Canyon Wilderness Desk: (435) 772-0170. Current advisories, water source status, and same-day permit availability are posted at the desk each morning. See ZION-FAQ-2026-01 for plain-language guidance.

# Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide

**Document No.:** ZION-NAR-2026-01
**Effective Date:** February 1, 2026
**Issuing Office:** Wilderness and Backcountry Office, Zion National Park

(continues in Section 1, Purpose and Scope) This guide describes permit requirements, trip options, and hazard management for travel in the Virgin River Narrows (the "Narrows").

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 1. Purpose and Scope

This guide describes permit requirements, trip options, and hazard management for travel in the Virgin River Narrows (the "Narrows"). It supplements ZION-BC-2025-03, *Backcountry and Wilderness Regulations*, which remains controlling on camping conduct, fires, and sanitation. Nothing in this guide authorizes travel during a permit suspension under Section 6.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Bottom-up day use" means travel upstream from the Temple of Sinawava, no farther than Big Spring, returning the same day.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Bottom-up day use"** means travel upstream from the Temple of Sinawava, no farther than Big Spring, returning the same day.
- **"Top-down through-hike"** means the 16-mile route from Chamberlain's Ranch to the Temple of Sinawava, in one or two days.
- **"Narrows campsite"** means one of the 12 numbered sites between Big Spring and the Chamberlain's Ranch trail segment.
- **"Flow rate"** means the discharge of the North Fork of the Virgin River in cubic feet per second (CFS) as measured at the USGS gauge near Springdale.

(continues in Section 3, Permit Requirements) Bottom-up day use to Big Spring requires no permit.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 3. Permit Requirements

3.1 Bottom-up day use to Big Spring requires no permit. Travel upstream of Big Spring without a top-down permit is prohibited.

3.2 All top-down through-hikes require a wilderness permit, whether completed in one day or with an overnight at a Narrows campsite.

3.3 Overnight through-hikes are limited to one night, at the specific numbered campsite on the permit. Party size at Narrows campsites is limited to 6 persons at sites 1 through 9 and 12 persons at sites 10 through 12.

3.4 Permits are issued under the calendar and drawing system described in ZION-BC-2025-03, Section 3.2. Overnight Narrows sites for the peak season (April through October 2026) are released on the 5th of the preceding month and are typically exhausted within one hour of release.

(continues in Section 4, Access) Chamberlain's Ranch is reached by an 18-mile dirt road outside the Park boundary, impassable when wet.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 4. Access

4.1 Chamberlain's Ranch is reached by an 18-mile dirt road outside the Park boundary, impassable when wet. No shuttle service is provided by the Park; commercial shuttles operate from Springdale under permit.

4.2 The exit is via the Riverside Walk to the Temple of Sinawava shuttle stop. During shuttle season (February 14 through November 29, 2026), private vehicles may not be left at the Temple of Sinawava; through-hikers must ride the canyon shuttle. See ZION-SH-2026-01, *Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice*.

4.3 The upper river crosses private land for the first three miles; camping, fires, and off-route travel are prohibited on this segment (fires are in any case prohibited throughout the route; see ZION-BC-2025-03, Section 4.1).

(continues in Section 5, Required and Recommended Equipment) Required for all top-down trips: footwear suitable for sustained in-water travel (open sandals are considered inadequate and issuance may be refused), and one waste containment kit per party per day (Section 7).

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 5. Required and Recommended Equipment

5.1 Required for all top-down trips: footwear suitable for sustained in-water travel (open sandals are considered inadequate and issuance may be refused), and one waste containment kit per party per day (Section 7).

5.2 Recommended: wooden or trekking staff, dry bags for all gear, and, at water temperatures below 55 °F, wetsuits or drysuits. Water temperature and flow are posted daily at the Wilderness Desk.

5.3 From November through April, drysuit-level protection is strongly recommended; hypothermia is the leading cause of Narrows rescues outside flood events.

(continues in Section 6, Flow and Weather Suspensions) Permits are not issued, and existing permits are suspended, when the flow rate exceeds 150 CFS.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 6. Flow and Weather Suspensions

6.1 Permits are not issued, and existing permits are suspended, when the flow rate exceeds 150 CFS. Between 120 and 150 CFS, permits are issued with a mandatory hazard briefing.

6.2 All Narrows travel, including bottom-up day use, is closed automatically upon issuance of a flash flood warning by the National Weather Service for the North Fork drainage. The Wilderness Desk may also suspend permits under a flash flood watch or when monsoon forecasting indicates significant risk.

6.3 Suspensions under this section are not eligible for fee refunds; permits may be rescheduled once, subject to availability, within the same season.

6.4 The Narrows drains a watershed extending 20 miles beyond the Park; storms not visible from within the canyon can produce flood pulses. Rising water, debris, or a sudden change in water color requires immediate movement to high ground.

(continues in Section 7, Sanitation) All solid human waste generated between Chamberlain's Ranch and the Temple of Sinawava must be packed out in a containment system.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 7. Sanitation

7.1 All solid human waste generated between Chamberlain's Ranch and the Temple of Sinawava must be packed out in a containment system. There are no toilets between the trailhead and Riverside Walk. Kits are distributed with each permit at no additional charge.

7.2 Urination directly into the flowing river channel is the accepted practice within the Narrows, contrary to general backcountry guidance, due to the absence of suitable soil.

(continues in Section 8, Cyanobacteria Advisory) Benign-appearing algal mats in the North Fork have periodically produced cyanotoxins.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 8. Cyanobacteria Advisory

8.1 Benign-appearing algal mats in the North Fork have periodically produced cyanotoxins. While an advisory is in effect, do not filter and drink river water; carry all drinking water, and prevent submersion of the head where practicable. Advisory status is posted at the Wilderness Desk and in ZION-FAQ-2026-01.

(continues in Section 9, Enforcement) Travel above Big Spring without a permit, camping at other than the assigned site, or failure to carry required equipment is punishable under 36 CFR 1.6. Violations recorded during flood suspensions are treated as aggravated due to rescue exposure.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 9. Enforcement

Travel above Big Spring without a permit, camping at other than the assigned site, or failure to carry required equipment is punishable under 36 CFR 1.6. Violations recorded during flood suspensions are treated as aggravated due to rescue exposure.

(continues in Section 10, Contact) Wilderness Desk: (435) 772-0170. Flow rate is available from the USGS gauge (09405500) and is posted daily at the visitor center and Wilderness Desk.

[Zion National Park — Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide]

## 10. Contact

Wilderness Desk: (435) 772-0170. Flow rate is available from the USGS gauge (09405500) and is posted daily at the visitor center and Wilderness Desk.

## 1. Purpose

This notice establishes the 2026 operating framework for the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive shuttle system and the associated private-vehicle restriction, issued under 36 CFR 1.5 and 4.30. It also summarizes access rules for the east side of the Park and the Kolob Canyons district.

(continues in Section 2, Definitions) - "Shuttle season" means February 14 through November 29, 2026, inclusive.

[Zion National Park — Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice, 2026]

## 2. Definitions

- **"Shuttle season"** means February 14 through November 29, 2026, inclusive.
- **"Scenic Drive"** means the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive from Canyon Junction to the Temple of Sinawava.
- **"Springdale Line"** means the town shuttle operating between Springdale and the Zion Canyon Visitor Center pedestrian entrance.
- **"Canyon Line"** means the park shuttle operating along the Scenic Drive with nine stops.

(continues in Section 3, Private Vehicle Restriction) During shuttle season, the Scenic Drive is closed to private vehicles.

[Zion National Park — Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice, 2026]

## 3. Private Vehicle Restriction

3.1 During shuttle season, the Scenic Drive is closed to private vehicles. Access to all Scenic Drive stops, including the Grotto (Angels Landing), Weeping Rock, and the Temple of Sinawava (Riverside Walk and Narrows), is by Canyon Line shuttle, bicycle, or foot.

3.2 The following are exempt from Section 3.1: registered guests of Zion Lodge, to the Lodge only; holders of accessibility placards issued at the visitor center, subject to daily availability; and administrative and emergency vehicles.

3.3 Outside shuttle season (November 30, 2026 through mid-February 2027), private vehicles may use the Scenic Drive; parking at trailhead lots is first-come and fills by mid-morning on holiday weekends.

(continues in Section 4, Shuttle Operations) Canyon Line service operates daily during shuttle season, beginning at 6:00 a.m. from the visitor center, with last departure from the Temple of Sinawava at 8:15 p.m. (7:15 p.m. before March 14 and after October 25).

[Zion National Park — Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice, 2026]

## 4. Shuttle Operations

4.1 Canyon Line service operates daily during shuttle season, beginning at 6:00 a.m. from the visitor center, with last departure from the Temple of Sinawava at 8:15 p.m. (7:15 p.m. before March 14 and after October 25). Frequency is 5 to 10 minutes midday.

4.2 No tickets or reservations are required for either line. Boarding is first-come at each stop.

4.3 Oversize items are limited to one item per passenger not exceeding 48 inches; canyoneering packs and Narrows staffs are permitted. Bear spray, firearms carried per applicable law, and fuel canisters must be secured in packs.

4.4 Pets are not permitted on shuttles, with the exception of service animals. This effectively limits visitors with pets to the Pa'rus Trail and areas outside the Scenic Drive during shuttle season.

4.5 Hikers exiting the Narrows after the final Canyon Line departure face a 8.5-mile walk to Canyon Junction; through-hike permit holders are advised to plan exits no later than two hours before final departure. See ZION-NAR-2026-01, Section 4.2.

(continues in Section 5, Bicycles) Bicycles, including class 1 e-bikes, are permitted on the Scenic Drive and the Pa'rus Trail year-round.

[Zion National Park — Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice, 2026]

## 5. Bicycles

5.1 Bicycles, including class 1 e-bikes, are permitted on the Scenic Drive and the Pa'rus Trail year-round. Class 2 and 3 e-bikes are restricted to the roadway.

5.2 Cyclists on the Scenic Drive must pull to the shoulder and place a foot on the ground when a shuttle approaches from behind; shuttles do not pass moving cyclists in the narrow segments.

5.3 Bicycles may not be ridden on any trail other than the Pa'rus, nor carried on any route requiring their portage over slickrock.

(continues in Section 6, East Side and Kolob Canyons Access) The Zion–Mount Carmel Highway (State Route 9) remains open to private vehicles year-round.

[Zion National Park — Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice, 2026]

## 6. East Side and Kolob Canyons Access

6.1 The Zion–Mount Carmel Highway (State Route 9) remains open to private vehicles year-round. Vehicles exceeding tunnel size limits (7 feet 10 inches in width or 11 feet 4 inches in height, including mirrors and accessories) require a tunnel escort permit ($15, valid for two passages), with escorted passage available 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. daily during 2026.

6.2 The Canyon Overlook Trail parking area holds approximately 30 vehicles; roadside parking outside marked spaces on Route 9 is prohibited and enforced by citation and towing.

6.3 Kolob Canyons Road (accessed from Interstate 15, exit 40) is open year-round, weather permitting, with winter closures after snowfall until plowed. The Kolob district has no shuttle and no fuel, food, or lodging services.

6.4 Kolob Terrace Road, serving the Subway trailheads and Lava Point, is not plowed above the Park boundary in winter; Lava Point Campground typically operates May through September. Camping and fire rules for Lava Point appear in ZION-BC-2025-03, Section 4.3.

(continues in Section 7, Parking and Congestion Management) The visitor center lot typically fills by 8:00 a.m. from March through October.

[Zion National Park — Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice, 2026]

## 7. Parking and Congestion Management

7.1 The visitor center lot typically fills by 8:00 a.m. from March through October. Visitors arriving later should park in Springdale (municipal fee lots) and use the Springdale Line, entering the Park on foot at the pedestrian bridge.

7.2 Stopping, standing, or parking on the roadway shoulder of Route 9 within Park boundaries outside marked areas is prohibited at all times.

# Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions

**Document No.:** ZION-FAQ-2026-01
**Effective Date:** March 1, 2026
**Issuing Office:** Division of Interpretation, Zion National Park

This document summarizes common visitor questions for 2026. It is informational; the referenced regulations control where any conflict exists.

(continues in Section 1, Getting Around) Q: Can I drive my car into Zion Canyon?

[Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 1. Getting Around

**Q: Can I drive my car into Zion Canyon?**
A: Not during shuttle season (February 14 through November 29, 2026). The Scenic Drive is shuttle, bicycle, and pedestrian only during that period. The free Canyon Line shuttle runs from the visitor center starting at 6:00 a.m. In winter, private vehicles may use the Scenic Drive. See ZION-SH-2026-01, *Shuttle Operations and Canyon Access Notice*.

**Q: Do I need a reservation just to enter the Park?**
A: No. Zion does not use a parkwide entry reservation in 2026. Specific activities require permits: Angels Landing (beyond Scout Lookout), all overnight backcountry trips, top-down Narrows trips, and technical canyons.

**Q: My RV is 12 feet tall. Can I drive Route 9 through the Park?**
A: You will need a tunnel escort permit ($15) for the Zion–Mount Carmel Tunnel if your vehicle is 7'10" wide or 11'4" tall or larger. Escorts run 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. daily.

(continues in Section 2, Angels Landing and the Narrows) Q: How do I get an Angels Landing permit?

[Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 2. Angels Landing and the Narrows

**Q: How do I get an Angels Landing permit?**
A: By seasonal lottery on Recreation.gov (applications roughly two months ahead) or the day-before lottery. The permit covers the section beyond Scout Lookout only; hiking to Scout Lookout requires no permit.

**Q: Do I need a permit to hike the Narrows?**
A: Bottom-up from the Temple of Sinawava as far as Big Spring: no permit. Top-down from Chamberlain's Ranch (day or overnight): permit required. Overnight sites sell out within about an hour of release on the 5th of the preceding month. See ZION-NAR-2026-01, *Narrows Trip Planning and Permit Guide*.

**Q: When does the Narrows close?**
A: Automatically whenever flow exceeds 150 CFS or the National Weather Service issues a flash flood warning. Spring snowmelt typically keeps flow above the threshold for several weeks in April and May. Check the gauge before traveling.

(continues in Section 3, Camping and Fires) Q: Can I have a campfire while backpacking in Zion?

[Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 3. Camping and Fires

**Q: Can I have a campfire while backpacking in Zion?**
A: No. Wood and charcoal fires are prohibited everywhere in Zion's backcountry, in every season, with no exceptions for fire rings, low fire danger, or winter. Only pressurized-fuel stoves are allowed, and even stoves may be suspended during a total fire ban. See ZION-BC-2025-03, Section 4.

**Q: What about at the campgrounds?**
A: Wood fires are allowed in the installed rings at Watchman and South campgrounds unless a posted restriction is in effect. Lava Point may be posted no-fire during dry periods.

**Q: Where can I camp for free outside a campground?**
A: Nowhere inside the Park without a wilderness permit, and permits carry fees. Dispersed camping is available on adjacent Bureau of Land Management lands outside Park boundaries, subject to BLM rules.

(continues in Section 4, Safety) Q: How much water should I carry?

[Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 4. Safety

**Q: How much water should I carry?**
A: On exposed summer routes, one gallon per person per day at minimum. Summer canyon temperatures regularly exceed 100 °F, and most heat casualties occur on the return leg of short, popular trails.

**Q: What is the cyanobacteria advisory?**
A: Algal mats in the Virgin River system periodically produce toxins that filtering does not remove. While an advisory is posted, do not drink filtered river water; carry all drinking water and avoid submerging your head. Status is posted at the visitor center.

**Q: Is Angels Landing dangerous?**
A: The route beyond Scout Lookout follows an exposed fin with chain assistance and unfenced drops exceeding 1,000 feet. Do not attempt it in wet, icy, or high-wind conditions, and do not take children who cannot maintain three points of contact unassisted.

(continues in Section 5, Wildlife and Pets) Q: Can I bring my dog?

[Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 5. Wildlife and Pets

**Q: Can I bring my dog?**
A: Pets are permitted only on the Pa'rus Trail (leashed, 6-foot maximum) and in developed areas and campgrounds. They are prohibited on all other trails, in the backcountry, and on shuttles.

**Q: Are there dangerous animals?**
A: Zion supports mountain lions, rattlesnakes, and, at higher elevations, black bears (rare). The most frequent wildlife incidents involve rock squirrels biting visitors who feed them, which is prohibited and subject to fine.

(continues in Section 6, Seasons) Q: What is the best time to visit?

[Zion National Park — Frequently Asked Questions]

## 6. Seasons

**Q: What is the best time to visit?**
A: April, May, September, and October offer moderate temperatures and full shuttle service. Summer brings extreme heat and monsoon flash-flood risk in the afternoons. Winter offers private-vehicle access to the canyon and light crowds; high-elevation trails hold ice, and traction devices are advised.

**Q: Is anything closed in 2026 I should know about?**
A: Closures change frequently with flow, storms, and rockfall; the visitor center posts current conditions each morning. Standing restrictions, including the private-land segment at the top of the Narrows and the prohibition on camping in the Left Fork corridor, appear in ZION-BC-2025-03, Section 5.
